pedagogy.summary: Probability as a fraction is the child's first symbolic representation of chance: for equally-likely outcomes, P(event) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes (P(6) = 1/6, P(heads) = 1/2). The teaching work is translating fluently between a situation, its probability fraction, and a position on the 0-to-1 scale, while holding onto the part-WHOLE meaning (favourable out of the total) rather than the more intuitive part-part ratio.
bestPractices: Derive the fraction from the equally-likely outcomes the child can see and count — six faces, one favourable → 1/6 — not as a rule to memorise

Insist on part-whole: the denominator is the TOTAL number of equally likely outcomes, the numerator the favourable ones; contrast explicitly with odds/ratio (1 red to 5 others is written 1/6, not 1/5)
Immediately place each fraction on the 0-to-1 scale so the symbol gains a magnitude (1/6 near 0, 1/2 at the middle)
Use reducible cases (26/52 = 1/2) to connect counting outcomes with equivalent fractions
Stress that favourable/total gives the probability only when outcomes are equally likely
keyRepresentations: favourable/total fraction written under the situation
0-to-1 probability scale with the fraction marked
Dice, coins, and bags with countable equally-likely outcomes
Area/part-whole diagrams linking the fraction to the whole set of outcomes
commonMisconceptions: Writing the probability as a part-part ratio/odds (1/5 or 1:5 for one red among six) instead of the part-whole fraction 1/6
Answering with a raw frequency or whole number ('3', or Fischbein & Gazit's '3/4 and 4/3') rather than favourable-over-total
Swapping numerator and denominator — putting the total on top
Applying favourable/total to situations whose outcomes are not equally likely

learn.summary: Help 9-10 year-olds write the probability of an equally-likely event as the part-whole fraction favourable/total (P(6)=1/6, P(heads)=1/2, one of three equally represented colours = 1/3), and translate fluently between a situation, its fraction, and a point on the 0-to-1 scale. The central work is holding the part-WHOLE meaning (favourable out of the TOTAL) against the more intuitive part-part ratio/odds, and attaching the symbol to a magnitude on the scale.

activities.title: Build the fraction from a bag, and place it on the 0-to-1 line
feedback: If a child writes 1/5 for one red among six: recount the whole set aloud including the red — the bottom number is every counter that could be drawn (6), not just the others (5).
If a child swaps to 6/1 or puts the total on top: a probability is never bigger than 1, so the whole (total) sits on the bottom and the favourable part on top.
When the counters change and both the fraction and marker move, name it: 'The symbol and its position on the scale moved together.'
activities.rationale: The topic is translation across three linked representations (situation ↔ fraction ↔ point on the scale). An editable bag whose fraction recomputes and whose marker slides makes the translation visible and reversible, and deriving the fraction from countable equally-likely outcomes keeps it meaningful rather than memorised.
sourceClaims: Probability of an equally-likely event is written as the part-whole fraction favourable/total (e.g. P(red)=1/6), expressed as a fraction, decimal or percentage — not as an integer.

Children reason more naturally with part-part ratios than part-whole fractions, and a documented additive error (Fischbein & Gazit) is giving the frequencies of outcomes as the probability (answering '3/4 and 4/3'), rather than favourable-over-total.
learnerActions: Fill a bag with coloured counters that are identical apart from colour, which you can see and count, and that will be drawn without looking — e.g. drop in one red among six total.
Write the probability of drawing red as a fraction: count the favourable (reds) for the numerator and the WHOLE set (all counters, red included) for the denominator, giving 1/6.
Mark that fraction on a 0-to-1 line (1/6 hugging 0, 1/2 at the middle).
Add more reds and re-count: watch the fraction change and the marker slide up the line together.
Deliberately test the wrong answer: try to make it 1/5 (red to the other five) and re-count the total to see the denominator counts all six counters, not the leftovers.
activities.intendedInsight: The denominator is the total number of equally likely outcomes (every counter that could be drawn), not the count of the OTHER outcomes; the fraction has a size you can locate between 0 and 1.

activities.title: Interpret a given fraction: what does each number count?
feedback: If the child says 6 is 'the other faces' or 'the ones that aren't 6': the 6 counts every face, including the favourable one.
Prompt: 'In 1/6, why is 6 on the bottom and not 5? What is the 6 counting?'
Prompt: 'Could this fraction ever be bigger than 1? Why or why not?'
activities.rationale: Interpreting a prepared fraction cleanly separates reading the symbol from constructing it, and tap-to-reveal makes the part-whole structure explicit. This is a scaffold for the interpret half; on its own it does not require the child to construct a fraction from a new situation.
sourceClaims: Probability of an equally-likely event is written as the part-whole fraction favourable/total (e.g. P(red)=1/6), expressed as a fraction, decimal or percentage — not as an integer.
learnerActions: Look at a fair six-sided die alongside the statement P(rolling a 6) = 1/6.
Say what the 1 stands for (one favourable face) and what the 6 stands for (the total number of equally likely faces).
On a labelled die or bag, tap the favourable outcomes to reveal the numerator, then tap the whole set to reveal the denominator.
Then reveal where that fraction sits on the 0-to-1 scale.
activities.intendedInsight: In favourable/total, the numerator counts the outcomes you want and the denominator counts ALL equally likely outcomes; the fraction names a magnitude on the scale.

activities.title: Construct and translate from a fresh situation
feedback: If the child writes 3/2 or 3:2: recount the whole set aloud including the reds — the denominator is every counter that could be drawn (5), so the total goes on the bottom, not the leftovers (2).
If the child answers with a raw count ('3'): a probability is always a part of the whole, written as a fraction (or decimal/percent) between 0 and 1, never a plain count.
P(red) and P(not red) together should make 1 (whole bag); use this to check the fraction (here 3/5 and 2/5).
For 26/52: counting 26 favourable of 52 total gives the same value as 1/2 — the equivalent fraction.
activities.rationale: Constructing favourable/total from a fresh situation exercises the translation the topic requires and surfaces the part-part misconception documented in the literature; reducible and simple fair cases link outcome-counting to equivalent fractions.
sourceClaims: Children reason more naturally with part-part ratios than part-whole fractions, and a documented additive error (Fischbein & Gazit) is giving the frequencies of outcomes as the probability (answering '3/4 and 4/3'), rather than favourable-over-total.
Probability of an equally-likely event is written as the part-whole fraction favourable/total (e.g. P(red)=1/6), expressed as a fraction, decimal or percentage — not as an integer.
learnerActions: Take a bag holding 3 red, 1 blue and 1 green counter (5 in total).
Write the probability of drawing red as a fraction, forming favourable-over-total: 3/5.
Mark 3/5 on a 0-to-1 scale (a little above the halfway point).
Then write the probability of NOT red and check what the two fractions add up to.
Try another fair case: a bag with three equally represented colours gives P(one colour) = 1/3, marked a little below the halfway point on the scale.
Reduce a case where it applies: a standard 52-card deck has 26 red cards, so P(red) = 26/52 = 1/2 — connect counting outcomes to equivalent fractions.
activities.intendedInsight: Building the fraction from a NEW situation — not reading a prepared one — is where part-whole understanding shows: a part-whole reasoner writes 3/5, a part-part reasoner writes 3/2 or 3:2 (red to non-red).

activities.title: Check the outcomes are equally likely before counting
feedback: If a child writes a simple fraction for an uneven spinner as if the regions were equal: check first that outcomes are equally likely; if they aren't, the colour counts are not the counts of equally likely outcomes, so favourable/total does not apply directly.
activities.rationale: Best practice stresses that favourable/total is valid only for equally-likely outcomes; making this check explicit guards against misapplying the rule.
learnerActions: Before writing favourable/total, ask: are all the outcomes equally likely?
Compare a fair die or a bag of identical counters (equally likely) with an uneven spinner whose regions differ in size (not equally likely).
For the uneven case, notice why counting colours or regions does not directly give the probability.
activities.intendedInsight: favourable/total gives the probability only when the outcomes are equally likely; otherwise the counts of colours/regions are not counts of equally likely outcomes.

activities.title: Talk it through: why that number on the bottom?
feedback: Catch a part-part answer and ask the child to recount the whole set.

For the 3 red, 1 blue, 1 green bag: if they say adding two greens doesn't change anything, the total (denominator) grows from 5 to 7 while the reds (numerator) stay at 3, so the probability of red falls from 3/5 to 3/7.
activities.rationale: Socratic prompts surface part-whole reasoning and misconceptions in the child's own words. Discussion supports the symbol work but linking symbol to magnitude is better shown on a scale than only talked about.
learnerActions: Answer a prompt such as 'What goes on the bottom of the fraction, and why?'
If you give a part-part answer, re-count the whole set and explain which outcomes the denominator includes.
Using your 3 red, 1 blue, 1 green bag, explain whether adding two more green counters would change the probability of red, and which number in your fraction changes.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating that the denominator counts the whole set of equally likely outcomes consolidates part-whole reasoning.

constraints: favourable/total gives the probability only when outcomes are equally likely; always check this first and do not apply it to uneven spinners or weighted situations.

The denominator is the TOTAL number of equally likely outcomes (favourable included), not the count of the other outcomes — contrast explicitly with odds/ratio (1 red to 5 others is 1/6, not 1/5 or 1:5).

A probability is a part of the whole from 0 to 1 inclusive: never a raw count (the only whole-number probabilities are 0 for impossible and 1 for certain), and never greater than 1 (so the total goes on the bottom, and the favourable count on top can be at most equal to it).

Tap-to-reveal and interpret-only tasks are scaffolds for reading a fraction; they do not require the child to CONSTRUCT a fraction from a new situation, which is where part-whole understanding is revealed.
Recognition/fill-in formats assess and rehearse translation directions but should be paired with construction from a fresh situation.
Place each fraction on the 0-to-1 scale so the symbol gains a magnitude (1/6 near 0, 1/3 below the middle, 1/2 at the middle).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source assessment lists '3/2 or 3:2' as the part-part error for 3 red among 5 (red-to-non-red = 3:2). This is internally consistent; retained as the misconception example.
A numerator/denominator swap depends on the situation: for 1/6 the swap is 6/1, for 3/5 it is 5/3. Feedback was kept matched to each activity's own setup.
The 1/3 example (one of three equally represented colours), present in the original objective, was restored to the construct activity and the scale-placement constraint.

The original claim that '3D adds no leverage' for symbolic probability was removed as a catalog-fit judgement rather than an established pedagogical law; probability as a fraction is handled well with countable physical/visual outcomes without asserting any medium is universally useless.

Self-audit of arithmetic/examples: 1 of 6 → 1/6; 3 of 5 → 3/5 (above halfway); one of three equal colours → 1/3 (below halfway); 26 of 52 → 1/2; P(red)+P(not red)=3/5+2/5=1; adding two greens to the 5-counter bag gives 3/7. All consistent. Fischbein & Gazit '3/4 and 4/3' quoted exactly from the source.

probeDeeper: In 1/6, why is 6 on the bottom and not, say, 5? What is the 6 counting?
You wrote the probability of red — now write the probability of NOT red. What do the two fractions add up to?
If I added two more green counters to the bag, would the probability of red change? Which number in your fraction changes?
Could this fraction ever be bigger than 1? Why or why not?
assess.correctAnswer: Interpret: the 6 is the total number of equally likely outcomes (the six faces), the 1 is the number of favourable outcomes (one face shows a 6). Construct: P(red) = 3/5 (three red out of five counters altogether), marked a little above the halfway point on the 0-to-1 scale.

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes the probability as a part-part ratio/odds (favourable to unfavourable) instead of the part-whole fraction — e.g. 3/2 or 3:2 for 3 red among 5
errorPatterns.nextMove: Recount the WHOLE set aloud including the reds; the denominator is every counter that could be drawn, so the total (5), not the leftovers (2), goes on the bottom
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the construct step writes red-to-others (3/2, or 1/5 for one red of six) rather than favourable-over-total

errorPatterns.pattern: Gives a raw frequency or whole number rather than a fraction ('3', or three-out-of-five spoken but written as an integer)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model that a probability is always a part of the whole, written as a fraction (or decimal/percent) between 0 and 1, never a plain count
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers with a count or a non-fraction; cannot express favourable-over-total as a single fraction

errorPatterns.pattern: Applies favourable/total to a situation whose outcomes are not equally likely
errorPatterns.nextMove: Check first that the outcomes are equally likely; if not, the counts of colours are not the counts of equally likely outcomes and favourable/total does not apply directly
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes a simple fraction for an uneven spinner or weighted situation as if the regions were equal

responseLevels.gap: Gives a whole-number count or cannot form a fraction; cannot say what the numerator and denominator represent, nor place a probability on the scale
responseLevels.full: Both interprets and CONSTRUCTS favourable/total from a new situation (3/5), checks the outcomes are equally likely, and marks the fraction at the right magnitude on the 0-to-1 scale
responseLevels.partial: Interprets a given fraction correctly and writes favourable/total for the easiest unit-fraction cases (1/6, 1/2), but on a fresh situation writes part-part odds, swaps numerator and denominator, or applies the fraction where outcomes are not equally likely

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two moves. First INTERPRET: show a fair six-sided die and the written statement 'P(rolling a 6) = 1/6'. Ask the child what the 1 and the 6 each stand for. Then TRANSLATE/CONSTRUCT: hand them a bag holding 3 red, 1 blue and 1 green counter and ask them to write the probability of drawing red as a fraction, and mark it on a 0-to-1 scale. Watch the construction step closely.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Interpreting a given fraction can be recited; the construct step reveals whether the child forms favourable/TOTAL. A part-whole reasoner writes 3/5; a part-part reasoner writes 3/2 or 3:2 (red to non-red); others give a raw count ('3') or swap to 5/3. Building the fraction from a fresh situation, not reading a prepared one, is where the understanding shows.
